name: ios-swiftui
summary: iOS/iPadOS SwiftUI structure with clear app, feature, shared UI, design system, service, model, and test boundaries.
dependency_direction: App entry -> Features -> SharedUI / DesignSystem -> Services -> Models. Feature code should not import another feature's internals.

folders.responsibility: App entry, scene setup, root navigation, dependency assembly.
folders.allowed: App lifecycle, root coordinators, environment injection, top-level navigation.
folders.avoid: Feature business logic, API clients, reusable controls, model definitions.

folders.allowed: Feature views, view models, feature-local state, feature-local helpers.
folders.avoid: Cross-feature imports that bypass a public boundary.

folders.responsibility: Reusable SwiftUI controls that are not tied to one feature.
folders.allowed: Small reusable views, modifiers, empty/loading/error states.

folders.responsibility: Project UI tokens, platform UI rules, and component policy.
folders.allowed: Color and typography tokens, spacing, system component wrappers, and UI-system configuration supported by the confirmed target.
folders.avoid: UI-system or third-party wrappers that conflict with existing conventions or require unapproved dependencies.

folders.responsibility: API clients, persistence adapters, platform services, and integration boundaries.
folders.allowed: Network, storage, system service wrappers, dependency protocols.
folders.avoid: SwiftUI views and feature-specific presentation logic.

folders.responsibility: Domain models, DTOs, and shared value types.
folders.allowed: Codable types, domain state, value objects.
folders.avoid: Networking side effects or UI state machines.

folders.responsibility: Unit, integration, and UI test entry points.
folders.allowed: Focused tests for models, services, view models, and critical flows.
folders.avoid: Manual-only validation notes as a substitute for tests when tests are practical.

rules: Preserve the existing deployment target, build settings, navigation, design system, and component conventions before choosing new APIs.
Use native SwiftUI/system components, semantic colors and type, and SF Symbols when they fit the product, accessibility needs, and confirmed deployment target.
Follow existing shape, spacing, typography, and token conventions; add tokens only when repeated use or product requirements justify them.
Use custom effects and motion when they serve product intent and pass accessibility, performance, and compatibility checks; do not add them as generic decoration.
Do not install third-party UI libraries without explicit authorization and a demonstrated need.

Use Liquid Glass or another current Apple design language only when the confirmed target supports it, the product wants it, and current official documentation validates the approach; do not raise deployment targets or restyle an existing product by default.
Verify current Apple developer documentation before implementing newly introduced platform UI APIs.
When visual direction is incomplete, preserve existing design signals or propose a coherent option and label assumptions instead of waiting for a fixed second phase.
Record durable, confirmed UI rules in docs/project_preferences.md; mirror only explicit hard invariants into AGENTS.md.
validation: Use the iOS build/run/debug workflow when simulator verification is needed.
Validate visible changes with screenshots or simulator inspection when available and proportionate.
